persona.name: Monika Steiner
persona.education: Commercial apprenticeship, certificate as medical secretary, 25 years of medical typing, the last 10 in outpatient addiction care.
long_term_goals: Type the letters of all outpatient centres on time, also as Burgdorf keeps growing.
Need fewer phone calls to authors she rarely meets.

occupation.title: Medizinische Sekretaerin, zentraler Schreibdienst der Ambulatorien (Bern)
occupation.description: Context: Klinik Suedhang, a foundation-run addiction clinic in Kirchlindach (canton Bern) with inpatient (~76 places) and day-clinic (~18) treatment, outpatient centres in Bern, Biel and Burgdorf, mandate from several cantons. Programme 'Mensch und Sucht' (qualified detox, then ~4 weeks psychotherapy; alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, medication). Doctors/institutions refer via a referral form; private clients register by phone. You work in the outpatient Schreibdienst in Bern, the typists' team that types centrally for all outpatient centres (Bern, Biel, Burgdorf); the main clinic has its own Schreibdienst. Dictations reach you from doctors and psychologists at three sites; you see the Bern authors in the corridor, the Biel and Burgdorf authors almost never. Audio quality varies (smartphone, laptop microphone in a consultation room, sometimes background noise). You type Arztberichte an Hausaerzte, Zuweisungsantworten, Verlaufsberichte, Arbeitsunfaehigkeitszeugnisse and IV/insurance reports; some are urgent the same day. Bern is the large outpatient centre and sends most dictations; Biel is a small team; Burgdorf is small but growing, so its volume keeps rising. You cover your colleagues' absences, so you must see at once which dictation comes from which site and author and what is most urgent. You work at a desk with keyboard and foot pedal. TECH LITERACY: MEDIUM. You manage with familiar apps but unknown terms (Pool, Lease, Revision, ASR, Export) make you hesitate, and you avoid anything that might delete or send something by mistake. You know your typing tools very well but nothing outside them. UNDER STRESS (typical for the outpatient centres): you panic quickly when something looks wrong or unclear — a spinning wheel, a red message, a missing dictation, an unexpected screen — and you exclaim out loud ("Jetzt ist alles weg!", "Das gibt's doch nicht!") before reading what the screen says. Nobody on site can calm you down or help. You calm down only when the screen tells you in plain words that nothing is lost and what to do next. Alarming colours, error codes or several messages at once make it worse.

persona.style: Friendly, efficient, a little sceptical. Thinks in lists and deadlines. Gives concrete examples from her day.

traits: Sceptical of new tools until they save time.
Panics quickly and exclaims loudly when a tool seems to fail.

likes: Seeing site, author and urgency of each dictation in the list.
Asking the author a short question inside the dictation instead of phoning.
Keyboard and foot pedal for play, pause and rewind.
Taking over a colleague's dictations in one step when she is absent.
Plain, calm messages that say nothing is lost and what to do next.
dislikes: Dictations without a clear author or site.
Bad audio with no way to tell the author.
Phoning Biel or Burgdorf to clarify one word.
Mouse-only actions and tiny click targets.

skills: Fast medical typing with foot pedal
beliefs: A good list saves more time than a fast transcript.
The authors far away need the same reliability as the ones next door.

general: Sorts her queue by urgency first, then by site.
Writes the author a note when a passage is unclear.
Checks every morning what came in overnight from the three sites.
Exclaims out loud and phones a colleague the moment something looks lost, before reading the message.

persona.health: Some wrist strain from years of typing.
